lead: Thresholding picks one grey level for the whole image. Region segmentation does the opposite: it groups neighbouring pixels that already look alike. Region growing starts from one or more seed pixels and adds touching pixels that satisfy a rule. Region splitting starts with the whole image, cuts a region into four quadrants while it is not uniform, then merges adjacent pieces back. The output is a set of regions, useful for finding a tumour in a scan, land and crop patches in satellite data, or parts of a manufactured component on an inspection line.
prereq: You need: 4- and 8-connectivity from Unit 1 and the failure of a single cut from 4.4.

blocks.text: Seed and predicate. Pick a seed pixel (x_s,y_s). Its grey value is f(x_s,y_s). A pixel is allowed when the predicate P is true:

blocks.where: f(x,y) is the grey level at pixel (x,y); f(x_s,y_s) is the seed grey level; T is the tolerance in grey levels.

blocks.text: Here T=1 means values one grey level above or below the seed are accepted. Use 4-connectivity (up, down, left, right) or 8-connectivity (also diagonals) from Unit 1. A pixel enters the region only if it is already touching the region and P is true. Put accepted pixels in a queue and test their neighbours. Stop when the queue is empty. The result depends on the seed: a seed inside a dark object grows a dark region. With P fixed on the seed value, the accepted set is the connected component of the seed, so visit order does not change it. Order can change the result only when P uses statistics of the region grown so far, such as its running mean, or compares a pixel with its accepted neighbour instead of the seed.

Splitting. Start with the whole image as one region R. Define a uniformity predicate Q(R). The strict form is Q(R)=true when every pixel in R has the same grey level. For a natural image with noise, use the mean μ_R and standard deviation σ_R:

blocks.where: |R| is the number of pixels in R; f(x,y) is a grey level; μ_R is the mean grey level in R.
σ_R is the standard deviation of grey levels in R.

blocks.text: Q(R)=true if σ_R ≤ T_σ, where T_σ is a chosen tolerance in grey levels. A low σ_R means the region is nearly flat. If Q(R) is false, cut R into four equal quadrants. Test each quadrant with Q. Repeat. The cuts form a quadtree: the whole image is the root, and each split has four children. Stop a branch when Q is true or the region is one pixel.

Merging. Splitting alone leaves many small flat pieces. Merge two regions only when they are adjacent and Q(R1 ∪ R2) is true. Adjacent here means they share an edge; touching only at a corner is not enough. The predicate is tested on the union, not on each region separately: two flat regions can have different means, and their union may fail Q. Repeat merging until no pair of adjacent regions can be merged. Then check for any region that still fails Q; if one exists, split it and merge again. Stop when no split or merge is possible. Merging order matters too; a greedy merge can block a better later merge. Splitting gives quadtree leaves. Merging combines adjacent leaves, possibly from different parents, so each final region is a union of quadtree leaves, not itself a node of the tree. This is the split-and-merge method. It is used when objects have smooth interiors and weak edges, where an edge map from 4.2 has gaps.

examples.question: A 4×4 image has grey values, row 0 to row 3: 5 5 4 4; 5 6 4 9; 4 4 5 9; 3 3 3 9. The seed is (0,0) with value 5. The predicate is |f−5|≤1 and connectivity is 4. List the accepted pixels and give the region size.
steps: Accepted grey levels are 4, 5 and 6, because |4−5|=1, |5−5|=0 and |6−5|=1.
Start with region R={(0,0)} and queue [(0,0)].
From (0,1), accept (0,2)=4. (1,1)=6 is also touching and accepted.
Continue: (0,3)=4, (1,2)=4, (2,1)=4, (2,2)=5 are accepted through touching neighbours.

traps: Seed choice is part of the answer: a different seed can give a different region even with the same predicate.
Say clearly whether P is fixed on the seed value (order does not matter) or on the current region mean or an accepted neighbour (order can matter); state which one the question uses.
For region growing, P compares a pixel with the seed value unless the question defines P on the current region mean.
In split-and-merge, merge only adjacent regions, and test Q on the union R1 ∪ R2, not on R1 and R2 separately.
A quadtree split always makes four equal quadrants; do not split a region into arbitrary shapes.

quiz.q: Define a seed pixel and the predicate P in region growing.
quiz.a: A seed is the starting pixel (x_s,y_s). P is the rule that a touching pixel must satisfy, for example |f(x,y)−f(x_s,y_s)|≤T.

quiz.q: Two runs of the same region-growing algorithm give different borders only under what condition on P?
quiz.a: Only when P is defined on the evolving region, for example |f(x,y) − mean of region so far| ≤ T, or on an accepted neighbour. The mean changes as pixels are added, so the order of adding changes which pixels pass. With P fixed on the seed value, the accepted set is the connected component of the seed and order does not matter.

quiz.q: In the figure image, use seed (0,0)=5 and T=0 with 4-connectivity. How many pixels are in the region?
quiz.a: Only value 5 is accepted. The pixels are (0,0), (0,1) and (1,0); the other 5 at (2,2) is not touching. Count = 3.

quiz.q: A region has grey levels 4,5,6,5. Compute μ_R and σ_R. Use Q true if σ_R≤1.
quiz.a: μ_R=(4+5+6+5)/4=5. Squares of deviations are 1,0,1,0; mean square is 0.5; σ_R=√0.5=0.7071. Q is true.

quiz.q: Why is Q tested on R1 ∪ R2 during merging, not on R1 and R2 separately?
quiz.a: Two separately flat regions may have different means; their union can have a large spread and should not be merged. Testing the union enforces uniformity of the final region.

quiz.q: Compare one global threshold with region growing for an image with uneven lighting.
quiz.a: A global threshold uses one grey level everywhere, so uneven lighting breaks it. Region growing uses local touching pixels and a seed value, so it can follow a locally uniform object, but it needs seeds and can leak through weak boundaries.

quiz.q: What is stored in the quadtree of a split-and-merge segmentation?
quiz.a: The tree stores the splitting stage: each internal node is a region that was split into four children, and the leaves are the unsplit blocks. Merging then joins adjacent leaves, so final regions are unions of leaves.

beyond: Not for the exam. Seeded region growing is the base of several superpixel and interactive segmentation methods; SLIC, for example, instead clusters pixels on colour and position, k-means style, to get small uniform patches before classification. Graph cuts and mean-shift segmentation replace the simple predicate with colour and spatial costs. In medical imaging, seeded region growing is still used for interactive lesion outlining. Search next for SLIC superpixels, graph cuts segmentation, mean-shift segmentation and random-walker segmentation.
